topics: 🎼 Did They Know Midnight? — Rabbi Zeira and Rav Ashi on David's lyre and Moses' 'about midnight'
🙏 'Am I Not Pious?' — Levi and Rabbi Yitzḥak on what made David a ḥasid
😰 'Lest Sin Cause' — the dotted luleh, Jacob's fear of Esau, and the missing miracle of Ezra's day
🛡️ A Fence Until Midnight — why the Rabbis said ḥatzot and why the violator is 'liable to death'
🔗 Redemption Beside Prayer — Rabbi Yoḥanan vs. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi on the evening order
📜 Ashrei Three Times a Day — the alphabet, the open hand, the missing nun, and the angels' flights

overview.title: 📖 Overview: David's Piety and the Rabbis' Fence
overview.subtitle: Berakhot 4a–4b
overview.hebrewSource: אֵיזֶהוּ בֶּן הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא — זֶה הַסּוֹמֵךְ גְּאוּלָּה לִתְפִלָּה שֶׁל עַרְבִית
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf finishes the aggada of King David's war council, then revisits whether Moses and David knew the exact moment of midnight. It explores David's self-description as 'pious': rising while other kings sleep, dirtying his hands to permit wives to their husbands, and admitting error before his teacher Mefivoshet — while the dotted word 'luleh' shows he still feared that sin might forfeit his reward. The Gemara then returns to the mishna: the Rabbis' 'until midnight' is a protective fence, illustrated by the tired man coming home from the field. That baraita launches a dispute between Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi over whether the evening Shema precedes the Amida, and the daf closes with the merit of Ashrei, the flights of the angels, and Shema upon one's bed.

slides.title: 🎼 Who Knew When Midnight Was?
slides.subtitle: Three approaches to Moses' 'about midnight' (Ex. 11:4) and David's lyre
rows: Did not know — God said 'at midnight', Moses said 'about', so he was uncertain
Needed a sign: the north wind played his lyre at midnight — 'Awake, harp and lyre; I will wake the dawn' (Ps. 57:9)
Knew exactly — but said 'about' lest Pharaoh's astrologers miscalculate and call Moses a liar
Also knew — the lyre was only to wake him from sleep
Spoke at midnight of the 13th: 'tomorrow, like midnight now (כַּחֲצוֹת), I will go out' — a comparison, not an approximation

callout.label: The Master's rule:
callout.text: Accustom your tongue to say 'I do not know' (לַמֵּד לְשׁוֹנְךָ לוֹמַר אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ), lest you become entangled in deceit. The daf also completes the council of war: Benayahu ben Yehoyada is the Sanhedrin — called Kereti because decisive and Peleti because wondrous in its rulings — and Evyatar is the Urim VeTummim. They consulted Ahitophel, then the Sanhedrin, then the Urim VeTummim, and only then Yoav the general.

slides.title: 🙏 'Keep My Soul, for I Am Pious'
slides.subtitle: Levi and Rabbi Yitzḥak explain David's claim in Psalm 86; the Gemara tests it against the dotted luleh

lines.speaker: One sage
lines.text: David said: all the kings of East and West sleep until the third hour — but I, 'at midnight I rise to give thanks' (Ps. 119:62).

lines.speaker: The other
lines.text: Kings sit in honored groups — but my hands are soiled with blood, miscarried fetus, and placenta to render a woman pure for her husband. And I consult my teacher Mefivoshet on every ruling: 'Did I judge well? Convict well? Acquit well? Declare pure and impure well?' — and I am not ashamed.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: The verse: 'I speak Your testimonies before kings and am not ashamed' (Ps. 119:46). His name was really Ish Boshet, called Mefivoshet because he 'embarrassed' David in halakha. Because David accepted correction, he merited a son Kilav — really Daniel — who embarrassed Mefivoshet in turn (Prov. 23:15, 27:11).

lines.speaker: Objection
lines.text: Can David call himself pious? 'If only [luleh] I had believed to see the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living' (Ps. 27:13) is dotted — David doubted whether he had a share among the righteous!

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: He knew he was pious; he feared lest sin cause him to lose it (שֶׁמָּא יִגְרוֹם הַחֵטְא).

lines.speaker: Proof
lines.text: Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi: God promised Jacob 'I will guard you wherever you go', yet 'Jacob was very afraid' of Esau — lest sin cause. And 'until Your people cross... until the people You acquired cross' (Ex. 15:16): Israel deserved a miracle in Ezra's day like Joshua's, but sin caused its absence.

callout.label: Big idea:
callout.text: Piety, in David's mouth, is forgoing royal dignity for Torah and for other people — while never assuming the reward is guaranteed.

slides.title: 🛡️ Why 'Until Midnight'? The Rabbis' Fence
slides.subtitle: Whose reading of 'when you lie down' do the Rabbis of the mishna follow?

nodes.content: ❓ If the Rabbis read 'when you lie down' like Rabbi Eliezer, say 'until the end of the first watch'; if like Rabban Gamliel, say 'until dawn'. Why midnight?
💡 They agree with Rabban Gamliel — by Torah law, until dawn. 'Until midnight' is a fence to distance a person from transgression (לְהַרְחִיק אֶת הָאָדָם מִן הָעֲבֵירָה)

columns.label: Without the fence
columns.content: A man comes home from the field: 'I'll eat a little, drink a little, sleep a little, then recite Shema and pray' — sleep overtakes him and he sleeps all night.

columns.label: With the fence
columns.content: He goes straight to the synagogue: if he reads Scripture, he reads; if he learns Mishna, he learns; then Shema and prayer; then home to eat and bless.

nodes.content: ❓ The baraita adds: 'whoever transgresses the words of the Sages is liable to death.' Why say that here of all places?
Two answers: (1) the compulsion of sleep (אוֹנֶס שֵׁינָה) makes extra vigilance necessary; (2) to exclude the view that the evening prayer is optional — it teaches that it is obligatory

callout.label: Support:
callout.text: The baraita's order — 'recites Shema and prays' — supports Rabbi Yoḥanan: at night too, Shema comes before the Amida.

slides.title: 🔗 Redemption Beside Prayer: Two Amoraim, Two Orders
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yoḥanan: one who juxtaposes redemption to the evening prayer is assured a place in the World-to-Come

boxes.title: Rabbi Yoḥanan
items: Order at night: Shema, blessing of redemption, then the Amida
Logic: the redemption from Egypt began already in the evening, though it was completed only in the morning
Verse: 'lying down' is likened to 'rising' — just as in the morning Shema is followed by prayer, so at night

boxes.title: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
items: The prayers were instituted between the two Shemas: morning Shema, then the prayers, then the evening Shema
Logic: the evening redemption was not the full redemption, so there is no need to join it to prayer
Verse: just as the morning Shema is next to rising from bed, the evening Shema is next to lying down in bed

boxes.title: Objection and answer
items: Mar son of Ravina: at night there are two blessings after Shema — Hashkivenu interrupts between redemption and prayer!
Answer: since the Sages instituted Hashkivenu, it counts as one extended redemption (גְּאוּלָּה אֲרִיכְתָּא)
Just as 'Lord, open my lips' (Ps. 51:17), said before every Amida, counts as extended prayer rather than an interruption

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: The dispute can rest on logic (when did the redemption begin?) or on how to read 'when you lie down and when you rise'; either way, additions the Sages instituted are treated as part of the original blessing.

slides.title: 📜 Why Ashrei Three Times a Day?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Elazar in the name of Rabbi Avina: one who recites 'A Psalm of David' (Ps. 145) three times daily is assured the World-to-Come

steps.content: 1️⃣ Is it because the psalm runs through the alphabet? Then say Psalm 119, whose acrostic appears eight times over
2️⃣ Is it because of 'You open Your hand and satisfy every living thing' (145:16)? Then say the Great Hallel: 'Who gives bread to all flesh' (136:25)
3️⃣ Rather — because it has both: the acrostic and the praise of God's sustenance of all creation
4️⃣ Rabbi Yoḥanan: why is there no verse beginning with nun? Because of 'Fallen [nafla], she shall rise no more, the virgin of Israel' (Amos 5:2)

5️⃣ In the West they read it softly: 'She has fallen, but shall fall no more — rise, virgin of Israel!' Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: even so, David supported the fallen in the very next verse — 'The Lord upholds all who fall' (samekh)

callout.label: Also on the daf:
callout.text: Rabbi Elazar bar Avina: Michael arrives in one flight ('one of the seraphim flew to me'), Gabriel in two ('caused to fly swiftly'), Elijah in four, the Angel of Death in eight — and in a plague, one. And Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: even after Shema in the synagogue, it is a mitzva to recite it on one's bed — 'say to your heart upon your bed and be still' (Ps. 4:5).

summary.principle: Piety means going beyond the letter — rising at midnight, admitting error, joining redemption to prayer — while the Rabbis' 'until midnight' guards the tired from losing the mitzva altogether.

flowSteps.content: 🎼 Moses' 'about midnight' and David's lyre: Rabbi Zeira — both knew; Rav Ashi — 'like midnight tonight'
🙏 'Am I not pious?' — rising at midnight; soiled hands to purify wives; consulting Mefivoshet. The dotted luleh = fear lest sin cause loss
🛡️ The Rabbis hold like Rabban Gamliel; 'until midnight' is a fence for the tired man from the field; 'liable to death' teaches the evening prayer is obligatory

columns.content: 🔗 R' Yoḥanan: Shema → redemption → Amida (Hashkivenu = extended redemption)
🔗 R' Yehoshua ben Levi: prayers between the two Shemas; evening Shema next to bed

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Ashrei is said thrice daily for its acrostic and its 'open hand'; where the nun is missing, David upheld the fallen

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Zeira, why did Moses say 'about midnight' if he knew the exact moment?
o: Because God had told him only an approximate time
Lest Pharaoh's astrologers miscalculate and call Moses a liar
Because midnight is not a fixed moment
Because he was speaking on the night of the thirteenth
quiz.e: Rabbi Zeira holds that Moses knew precisely, but followed the Master's rule to accustom one's tongue to say 'I do not know', so that an error by Pharaoh's astrologers would not make him appear a liar.

quiz.q: Whose reading of 'when you lie down' do the Rabbis of the mishna actually follow, and why do they say 'until midnight'?
o: Rabbi Eliezer's; midnight is when the first watch ends
Rabban Gamliel's; midnight is a rabbinic fence to keep people from falling asleep first
Neither; they derive midnight from David's rising at midnight
Rabban Gamliel's; midnight is when priests finish eating teruma
quiz.e: The Gemara concludes the Rabbis hold like Rabban Gamliel that the Torah time extends until dawn, and they said 'until midnight' to distance a person from transgression, as the baraita of the man returning from the field illustrates.

quiz.q: According to the Gemara's 'logical' explanation, what is the point of dispute between Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi?
o: Whether the evening prayer is obligatory or optional
Whether the redemption from Egypt began already in the evening or only in the morning
Whether one may recite Shema after midnight
Whether Hashkivenu is a Torah-level blessing
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan holds redemption began in the evening (though completed in the morning), so redemption is joined to the evening prayer; Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds only the morning redemption was full-fledged, so there is no need.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara answer the objection that Hashkivenu interrupts between the blessing of redemption and the evening Amida?
o: Hashkivenu is recited silently and so does not count
Hashkivenu is recited after the Amida rather than before it
Since the Sages instituted it, Hashkivenu is considered one extended blessing of redemption
Rabbi Yoḥanan retracts and agrees with Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
quiz.e: Just as 'Lord, open my lips' before the Amida is treated as extended prayer, Hashkivenu, having been instituted by the Sages, is treated as an extended redemption blessing and not an interruption.

quiz.q: Why is Psalm 145 (Ashrei) singled out for recitation three times a day rather than Psalm 119 or the Great Hallel?
o: Because it is the shortest psalm of praise
Because it alone was composed by David
Because it contains both an alphabetical acrostic and the verse 'You open Your hand'
Because it is the only psalm missing a letter
quiz.e: Psalm 119 has an even fuller acrostic and the Great Hallel also praises God's sustenance, but only Ashrei combines the two features.
